clue.text: Small weeds jump from mule, maybe picked up here

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
to hoe is to weed, so 'weeds' gives the verb form
to hop is to jump

explanation.surface: A gardener's tiny weeds spring out of a mule, as if bought along with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mule' looks like the animal or a stubborn person, but here it is a backless slipper, and the definition describes where you would buy one.
explanation.definitionFit: A mule is a style of backless shoe, so it is the sort of item purchased at a footwear retailer.

clue.text: Spot anonymous driver on dam

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sitting on another comes above it, so the driver is written first

parts.note: The Stig is the masked, unnamed racing driver on the BBC motoring show Top Gear
a dam is an animal's mother, giving MA

explanation.surface: Catch sight of a mystery motorist parked on a reservoir wall.
explanation.walkthrough: Top Gear is a British TV car show whose test driver, The Stig, never shows his face.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma can be a mark or blemish on the skin, a spot in the literal sense.

clue.text: About a matter concerning the club bistro, etc up for renewal

definitions.text: About a matter concerning the club
definitions.note: an adjective phrase: relating to the business of being 'in the club', slang for pregnant

indicators.note: something up for renewal is to be remade, so the letters of the two fodder words are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A members' club's restaurant and other facilities are due for a lease renewal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the club' is British slang for pregnant, so 'the club' here is pregnancy, not a social club.
explanation.definitionFit: Obstetric medicine deals with pregnancy and childbirth, the condition slangily called being in the club.

clue.text: Artist in school that is likeable on the surface

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

indicators.note: the surface of a word is its outside, so only the first and last letters of likeable are kept

explanation.surface: A painter at an academy seems pleasant enough on the face of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Egon Schiele was an Austrian expressionist painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Egon Schiele was an early twentieth-century Viennese painter, an example of the general class named.

clue.text: Company promoted offensive group

indicators.note: in a down clue, being promoted sends the letters upwards, so they read from bottom to top

parts.note: the Tet Offensive was the 1968 North Vietnamese attack launched at the lunar new year festival

explanation.surface: A firm has advanced a group of people who give offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offensive' is not an adjective here but a noun, the military campaign named after the Vietnamese new year.
explanation.definitionFit: An octet is a set of eight, such as eight musicians performing together.

clue.text: Skinned two fish in distress

indicators.note: skinning strips the outer covering, here the front letter of each fish

parts.note: the char and the bass are both fish, the char a trout relative and the bass a perch-like sea fish

explanation.surface: Two fish are being gutted and skinned, presumably to their great distress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skinned' takes C off char and B off bass. The blog also allows five-letter fish such as charr and shark with both ends removed.
explanation.definitionFit: To harass someone is to pester and trouble them, synonymous with the verb meaning to upset or torment.

clue.text: Touching win secured by a good man

indicators.note: the win is held fast within the other two pieces, so it is placed between them

parts.note: ST, for saint, is the crossword stock abbreviation for a good man
to gain is to win or obtain

explanation.surface: An emotional victory has been clinched by a decent fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touching' looks like an adjective meaning moving, but it is the preposition meaning in contact with.
explanation.definitionFit: Something leaning against a wall is in contact with it, the prepositional sense of touching.

clue.text: Wow — ma'am dazzled regardless of the odds

indicators.note: the odd letters are disregarded, so only the even-numbered letters of the two words are kept

explanation.surface: A dazzled royal lady wins against all the odds, to everyone's astonishment.
explanation.definitionFit: To wow an audience is to astonish or astound them, a synonym used as a verb.

clue.text: Bronze gets dirty, unusually, top to bottom

indicators.note: the letter at the head of the down entry is shifted to its foot to give the invented word

parts.note: someone who unbathes, a made-up word, would undo a bath and so become dirty, an unusual way of saying it

explanation.surface: A bronze statue unusually collects grime from head to foot.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: move the top letter of the answer to the bottom and you get UNBATHES, a whimsical coinage for getting dirty.
explanation.definitionFit: To bronze is to tan the skin, which is what lying in the sun does.

clue.text: Dance, even if interrupting one following turn

indicators.note: the conjunction breaks into the follower, splitting it apart

parts.note: a fan is a follower or devotee
'and' can mean even if, as in the old phrase 'and it please you'
a go is a turn in a game

explanation.surface: A dance, even if it cuts in on someone following a turn.
explanation.definitionFit: The fandango is a lively Spanish courtship dance, an example of the general term.

clue.text: Show insight, adamant at changes after head of department is sacked

indicators.note: the letters change their positions, so the fodder is rearranged
being sacked means losing a place, so that letter is dropped from adamant
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A firm boss shows insight and alters course after a departmental chief is fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is sacked' removes D, the head of 'department', from ADAMANT, leaving AAMANT for the anagram. ITMA was a 1940s BBC radio comedy show.
explanation.definitionFit: It was a hugely popular wartime BBC radio comedy programme starring Tommy Handley, so it is a show.

clue.text: Post opened by sheepish female film star

indicators.note: the post is split open and the female placed inside it

parts.note: a mast is a tall upright post
a ewe is a female sheep

explanation.surface: A shy actress opens a letter from the morning post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sheepish' looks like it means shy, but it literally means of a sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: Mae West was a Hollywood actress of the 1930s famed for innuendo, so she is a screen celebrity.

clue.text: Dare, for example, one to get drink served up for woman

parts.note: Dan Dare is the space-pilot hero of the British comic Eagle, so Dare's first name is Dan
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: served up, in this across clue, means the drink is presented backwards

parts.note: ale is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone is daring a person to have a drink brought out to a lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Dan Dare is a 1950s British comic-strip spaceman, the hero of the Eagle.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniela is a female given name, so it stands for a woman in the usual crossword way.

clue.text: Go to here to act extravagantly on spare capital

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece put on another follows it

parts.note: spare time is free time, so spare means free

parts.words: Go to here to act extravagantly
parts.note: to go to town means to do something lavishly, so this place is town

explanation.surface: Someone is told to splash out in the capital on money they can spare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go to here' is an elaborate way of pointing at the word that completes 'go to town'.
explanation.definitionFit: Freetown is the capital city of Sierra Leone in West Africa.

clue.text: Where celebs are frequently working blind

parts.note: a machine that is on is working
a blind and a screen both shield a window or hide something

explanation.surface: Celebrities often seem to be working without seeing what they are doing.
explanation.definitionFit: Famous people are often seen on television or film, which is where the screen shows them.

clue.text: Run into walrus, maybe causing wreck

indicators.note: the run goes inside the moustache

parts.note: a walrus is a style of thick drooping moustache, and tash is British slang for a moustache
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Running into a walrus could cause a nasty crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'walrus' is not the animal but a bushy moustache, called a tash in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: To trash something is to wreck or destroy it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: It's blown by planner altering exterior of house

indicators.note: the rearranged letters form the outside, with the house letters inside them
the letters of planner are altered, that is, rearranged

explanation.surface: A planner's designs for the outside of a house are being dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's blown' reads like a ruined plan, but it is the definition: a thing that is blown.
explanation.definitionFit: An alpenhorn is a very long wooden Swiss wind instrument, which a herdsman plays by blowing.

clue.text: Lefty messed up — so what?

indicators.note: messed implies jumbled, so the fodder letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A left-winger shrugs off a mistake with a careless retort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lefty' suggests a left-wing politician, but it means a left-handed person; 'up' is part of the fodder, not of the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A southpaw is someone left-handed, especially a boxer, and lefty is an informal name for such a person.

clue.text: Former upper class to be arrested, not a moment too soon

indicators.note: the class letter is held within the other word, as if detained

parts.note: once means formerly, in a former time
U is the conventional label for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: A one-time aristocrat is about to be arrested, and about time too.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done right on time, exactly at the expected moment, is not a moment too soon.

clue.text: Perhaps name characters covering equestrian sports championship

indicators.note: the characters that cover a word are its outside letters, its first and last

parts.note: a title is a championship won in sport

explanation.surface: Perhaps someone names the riders contending for an equestrian title.
explanation.definitionFit: To entitle a book is to give it a name, so naming is one example of the verb.

clue.text: Photos containing old ladies, perhaps, providing high-level coverage?

indicators.note: the photos hold the other letters inside them

parts.note: snaps are informal photographs
WC, water closet, is a toilet such as the ladies

explanation.surface: Pictures featuring elderly women are meant to give a top-level overview.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ladies' is not women but a public toilet, WC.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow on mountain peaks covers their highest parts, coverage at a high altitude.

clue.text: After church, drink in gold castle

indicators.note: the rest follows the church abbreviation, so it comes first
the drink sits inside the gold

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
tea is a drink

explanation.surface: After a church service, someone has a drink in a golden castle.
explanation.definitionFit: A chateau is a French castle or grand country house.

clue.text: Sloppy kisser who may go downhill rapidly

definitions.note: a plural noun phrase: people who might hurtle down a slope

indicators.note: sloppy means messy, so the letters of kisser are messed up

explanation.surface: A slobbery kisser's love life might go rapidly downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go downhill' suggests decline, but here it is literal descent of a snowy slope.
explanation.definitionFit: Downhill racers on snow travel fast down mountains, which is exactly what such athletes do.

clue.text: In a short time, rogue is a bit of a swine

parts.note: T is the abbreviation of time, shortened to one letter
a rotter is a rogue or scoundrel

explanation.surface: Before long, a scoundrel turns out to be rather a swine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit of a swine' sounds like a mild insult, but it means a literal part of a pig.
explanation.definitionFit: A trotter is a pig's foot, so it is a part of the animal, a swine.

clue.text: Force stepping in over prisoner in camp

indicators.note: the force letter steps in between the two other pieces

parts.note: O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over
an old lag is a seasoned prisoner, so lag is slang for a convict
F is the physics abbreviation for force

explanation.surface: Force is used, stepping in over a prisoner held in a camp.
explanation.walkthrough: An Oflag was a German WWII prison camp for officers, as in Colditz.
explanation.definitionFit: Oflag was a German prisoner-of-war camp for captured officers in the Second World War.

clue.text: Bohemian family turning on switch

indicators.note: in an across clue the turned family placed on the switch comes after it

parts.note: to switch someone is to whip them, to beat

indicators.note: turning round makes the family read backwards

parts.note: kin are one's family

explanation.surface: An unconventional relative turns the switch on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'switch' looks like a light switch, but it is the cane, as a verb meaning to whip.
explanation.definitionFit: A beatnik was a 1950s nonconformist, an artistic person living unconventionally, like a bohemian.

clue.text: Don't declare staff

definitions.meaning: in cricket, to ... is to keep batting rather than declare the innings closed
a stick, like a conductor's or relay runner's rod

explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it means keep batting, the opposite of declaring in cricket; as one word, a short rod or staff.

clue.text: Attract hanky-panky with anybody? — you're kidding me

parts.note: to pull is to attract, especially a partner
'a bit of the other' is British slang for sex
one is a pronoun meaning anyone, as in 'one never knows'

explanation.surface: Someone claims to lure anyone at all into a fling, and the listener doesn't believe it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The other' is British slang for sexual activity.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom expresses disbelief, telling the speaker they must be joking.

clue.text: Cycle maker found in middle of canal in punt

indicators.note: the central letter is found inside the bet

parts.note: a punt is a bet, a wager

indicators.note: the middle of a five-letter word is its third letter

explanation.surface: A bicycle manufacturer is discovered in a punt halfway along a canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycle' looks like a bicycle, but it is the Ring cycle of four operas; 'punt' is a bet, not a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Wagner composed the Ring, a cycle of four operas, so he made a cycle.

clue.text: Medication found in extremely unclean toilets around university

definitions.note: a mass noun standing for the plural ointments

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters
the toilets surround the university letter

parts.note: the gents is a men's public toilet in Britain

explanation.surface: Remedies are discovered in some filthy toilets near a campus.
explanation.walkthrough: The gents is the British name for a men's public toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Unguents are ointments or salves applied to the skin, so they are a kind of medical treatment.
